indicators.note: around suggests the letters of the next word are turned about and rearranged

explanation.surface: A tough coastal grass grows all around a harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' looks like a placing word, but here it tells you to rearrange the letters of 'seaport'.
explanation.definitionFit: Esparto is a tough, wiry grass from Spain and North Africa used for rope and paper.

clue.text: Tail on wounded mice confined to particular area

parts.note: a tail is the end of something

indicators.note: wounded means hurt or knocked about, so the letters of mice are mixed up

explanation.surface: A wounded mouse with its tail hanging off is stuck in one small patch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' puts the tail at the front here, and 'wounded' is the anagram signal, not part of the picture of an injured mouse.
explanation.definitionFit: A disease or species found only in one region is described as native to that region and nowhere else.

indicators.note: spread means scattered about, so the letters of the two following words are mixed

explanation.surface: A street painter is asked whether he daubs dull, flat paint across the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: 'spread' is the anagram signal, and the person it describes spreads paint on the street.
explanation.definitionFit: A pavement artist draws chalk or paint pictures on the street for passers-by.

clue.text: Provider of true line for dynasty

definitions.meaning: a straight-edge used to draw a true, straight line
the reign or period of government of a ruling house

explanation.definitionFit: A rule is a ruler for drawing straight lines, and also the reign of a ruling house over a country.

parts.note: OP is the abbreviation of opus, a musical work
the press means the newspapers

explanation.surface: Someone is buried under paperwork at the office.
explanation.definitionFit: To oppress is to weigh down or crush someone, much as being overwhelmed does.

clue.text: Eg Chesterfield, up to now not finished

indicators.note: not finished means the final letter of the phrase is cut off

parts.note: up to now means so far, until the present

explanation.surface: A sofa is still unfinished in the upholsterer's workshop.
explanation.walkthrough: A Chesterfield is a deep-buttoned leather couch, not the English town the capital suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: A Chesterfield is a classic padded couch with arms the same height as its back.

clue.text: Unlicensed premises? Keep quiet, English have visited!

parts.note: sh is the sound used to tell someone to be quiet
have been means have visited, as in 'I have been to Rome'

explanation.surface: A bar owner hisses for silence because English drinkers have dropped in.
explanation.walkthrough: A SHEBEEN is an Irish or Scottish word for an illegal drinking den.
explanation.definitionFit: A shebeen is an illicit bar selling drink without a licence.

parts.note: fat is greasy, oily matter
E is the abbreviation for earth, as on electrical wiring

explanation.surface: The future of greasy soil is in question.
explanation.definitionFit: Fate is the power believed to decide what will happen, much like one's destiny.

parts.note: shy of means short of or lacking
a lock is a hold that clinches, as in wrestling

explanation.surface: A heartless lender is missing the final decisive move.
explanation.walkthrough: SHYLOCK is the moneylender in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice, who demands his pound of flesh.
explanation.definitionFit: Shylock is the merciless moneylender in Shakespeare, and his name is used for any ruthless lender.

clue.text: Condition of PC-down and out underneath the arches!

definitions.text: Condition of PC-down and out underneath the arches!

parts.words: Condition of PC-down and out underneath the arches
parts.note: a policeman is a flatfoot, and someone with fallen arches has flat feet; 'down and out under the arches' paints a homeless person sleeping beneath railway arches

explanation.surface: A policeman finds himself homeless, sleeping rough beneath the railway arches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down and out underneath the arches' sounds like sleeping rough, but it means the arches of the feet have fallen.
explanation.definitionFit: Fallen arches give flat feet, and flatfoot is slang for a policeman on the beat.

clue.text: How to improve the mind in evolutionary terms?

definitions.meaning: read as two words, to ... is to grow one's mind
with regard to growth and development over time

explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it means growing in mind; as one word it means with regard to growth and maturing stages.

indicators.note: dual means two of something, so the motorway is written twice

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main motorway, written here with the 1 as the letter I

explanation.surface: A free-spirited traveller drives along a two-lane highway.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the London-to-Leeds motorway; its figure 1 is read as an I. MIMI is the heroine of Puccini's opera La Bohème.
explanation.definitionFit: Mimi is the seamstress heroine of Puccini's opera La Bohème, so she is a character from the Bohemian world.

indicators.note: in both directions means the word reads the same forwards and backwards

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A flat surface stretches out either way.
explanation.definitionFit: A level surface is even and horizontal, with no bumps or slope.

indicators.note: in means one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: OO looks like a pair of glasses
TT stands for teetotal, a person who drinks no alcohol

explanation.surface: A man who never drinks is wearing glasses.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto is a man's first name.

clue.text: Tartan attributed to head of Picts

indicators.note: head of means the first letter of the following word

parts.note: laid, as in blame laid at someone's door, means attributed

explanation.surface: A tartan pattern is credited to a chieftain of the ancient Picts.
explanation.walkthrough: The Picts were ancient people of Scotland, which suits the tartan picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaid is the checked woollen cloth of Scottish dress, much like tartan.

clue.text: Raised we hear, and risen we hope!

indicators.note: we hear means the word is judged by how it sounds when spoken

parts.note: bred means raised or reared, as children or animals

explanation.surface: A baker hopes the dough has come up in the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: Dough rises in the oven if the yeast works, so 'risen, we hope' describes a loaf.
explanation.definitionFit: A loaf is made with yeast so that the dough rises before and during baking.

indicators.note: without means the following letters are taken out

parts.note: OO looks like a pair of glasses

explanation.surface: Lovers kiss and cuddle once they have taken off their glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the OO, a picture of spectacles, from CANOODLES.
explanation.definitionFit: Luminaries are sources of light, and wax lights give a gentle glow.

parts.note: the eastern English county famous for its Broads, waterways and wide flat views

explanation.definitionFit: Norfolk is an English county known for the Broads, its network of rivers and lakes, and its wide, flat landscape.

parts.note: a spa is a mineral spring or well
to ring is to telephone

explanation.surface: Someone means well and gives a phone call.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean well' reads as one phrase, but 'Mean' is the definition, as in stingy.
explanation.definitionFit: Being stingy with money or effort is careful or frugal economy.

clue.text: Poet with his hands continually in his pockets?

definitions.text: Poet with his hands continually in his pockets?

parts.words: Poet with his hands continually in his pockets?
parts.note: names an English poet whose surname also means one who keeps reaching into his pockets to pay out money

explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Spender was an English poet, and his surname also describes someone who freely lays out money.

indicators.note: changes means the letters of the next word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Harsh officials quiz people about changes in postal rates.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gestapo was the Nazi secret police, notorious for brutal questioning.

clue.text: Soup, for example, is official at many courses

definitions.meaning: the first course of a meal
the person who sets a race going at a racecourse

explanation.definitionFit: A first course such as soup opens a meal, and the official who fires the gun begins a race at a racecourse.

clue.text: … not a direct delivery by air.

definitions.text: … not a direct delivery by air.

parts.words: not a direct delivery by air
parts.note: a cricket ball that curves through the air rather than travelling straight

explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a ball that curves in flight, rather than going straight, is bowled by a seam or swing bowler.

definitions.meaning: connected by blood or marriage, kin

explanation.definitionFit: To relate is to narrate, and kin by blood belong to one clan.

indicators.note: served means dished out, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: tea's is read as the plural teas

explanation.surface: Ordinary food arrives when the afternoon tea is brought out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'served' tells you to rearrange the letters of TEAS.
explanation.definitionFit: Eats is a colloquial word for food, grub in everyday speech.

clue.text: A foot, we hear, in a jug

parts.note: jug and stir are both slang for prison

explanation.surface: A foot is said to be stuck in a pitcher.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sounds like 'afoot', meaning up and about. In jug and in stir both mean in prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Astir means up and moving about, the same as afoot when said out loud.

clue.text: I have old fashioned object of love

indicators.note: fashioned means shaped or made anew, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone owns an old-fashioned thing they adore.
explanation.walkthrough: The newspaper text misread I as L. 'fashioned' rearranges OLD into DOL, which follows the I; 'have' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: An idol is someone or something greatly adored or worshipped.

clue.text: Not exposed to view in arms rising

indicators.note: rising in a down clue means the word is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: arms means weapons such as guns

explanation.surface: Weapons are kept hidden while a rebellion grows.
explanation.definitionFit: Snug means cosy and sheltered, tucked away from sight.

indicators.note: taken from means the letters are lifted out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Cash has been stolen from the church collection.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelf is an old, disapproving word for wealth or riches.

clue.text: Land in nets, get me free by 'such means?

definitions.text: Land in nets, get me free by 'such means?

indicators.note: free means let loose, so these letters are released and rearranged

explanation.surface: A fish caught in netting begs to be set loose.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is definition and wordplay: 'free' rearranges LAND IN NETS GET ME, and freeing something caught in nets is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Freeing something from a tangle of nets is untangling it, setting it loose.

indicators.note: element means a part of the word that follows, which holds the letters

explanation.surface: Someone plays down the infectious part of an illness.
explanation.walkthrough: AGIO is a banking term for the charge or discount on exchanging money.
explanation.definitionFit: Agio is the percentage charged when exchanging currency, a premium or discount on the face value.

annotationWithheld.why: Renounced safety-device overdrawn: FUSE inside RED gives the letters, but no clue word signals the container; only 'overdrawn' could, and it already supplies RED
